segments.text: Back in the 1980s, France, the United Kingdom, Germany, Italy, and Spain were discussing
the development of a new European fighter.
There was agreement on one thing, the aircraft needed to perform both air-to-air and surface
attack missions.
The disagreement was over how much priority each mission should receive.
France wanted a lighter aircraft with a more balanced emphasis between air combat
and ground attack.
The United Kingdom, Germany, Italy, and Spain placed greater emphasis on air superiority.
In 1985, France left the joint program and moved forward with its own aircraft.
There was another very specific requirement as well.
The new French fighter had to meet the needs of French carrier aviation.
That requirement eventually produced the Rafale family.
There was the Rafale C, the single-seat land-based version, the two-seat Rafale B, and the Rafale
M, designed to operate from aircraft carriers.
The Rafale entered service with the French Navy in 2004 and with the French Air Force
two years later.
The Typhoon followed a different path and entered RAF service in 2003.
Its development placed heavy emphasis on air defense while its ground attack capabilities
were expanded progressively over time.
That difference in priorities helps explain the two aircraft.
But it doesn't mean one was designed exclusively for air combat while the other
was designed exclusively as a multirole fighter.
In a British case, that emphasis on air defense is still very visible in the way
the aircraft is used operationally.
The Typhoon is part of the UK's Quick Reaction Alert and also takes part in NATO
air policing missions.
And in that kind of mission, reaction time, availability, climb performance, and interception
capability matter directly.
When it comes to the engines, the Typhoon also produces higher numbers.
Each EJ-200 can generate roughly 90 kN of thrust with afterburner.
Together that's around 180 kN.
The Rafale's two M88 engines together produce somewhere around 147 kN.
So, in terms of maximum thrust, the number favors the Typhoon.
But by itself, that tells us very little about actual performance.
Weight, altitude, fuel load, weapons, and aerodynamic drag can completely change how
an aircraft behaves.
A clean fighter performing at an airshow is not going to behave the same way when it's
loaded for combat.
When we move to sensors, the clearest difference between the versions we've chosen is the radar.
The Rafale F-3R uses the electronically scanned RBE-2A AESA.
The Typhoon FGR-4 we're looking at here uses the mechanically scanned CAPTUR-M.
And at this specific point, the Rafale has a technological advantage.
An AESA radar gives the aircraft greater flexibility in how it manages its beam and
handles different search and tracking tasks.
But that doesn't translate into some fixed detection distance.
Who detects whom first depends on a combination of factors – position, altitude, the target's
radar signature, electronic interference, radar mode, and information coming from other platforms.
The publicly available sources also don't provide a direct test under identical conditions
that would allow us to say one aircraft would always detect the other first.
The British Typhoon adds another piece to that equation with PIRATE, an infrared search
and track system that can search and track targets passively without relying on radar
emissions.
When it comes to long-range air-to-air weapons, the two fighters share one major capability
– METEOR.
The missile was designed to retain energy throughout much of its flight, particularly during
the final phase of an interception.
So METEOR doesn't really break the tie here – both fighters can use it.
Up to this point, the clearer difference is somewhere else.
The Typhoon still has a strong orientation towards interception and air defense.
The Rafale F3R we're using in this comparison has a specific advantage in radar
architecture.
But in a real combat environment, none of these systems operates in isolation.
External sensors, electronic warfare support, other aircraft, the quality of the information
available to the pilot, and the weapons being carried can matter just as much.
